claim: A fully-stacked agent composing many quality/alignment patterns (perceive, decompose, plan, vote, audit, reflect, constitution-check, audit side-effects, provenance-track, explain) can cost 50-100x a single raw model call, making cost a first-class design constraint, not an afterthought.
stance_target: zero-hallucination/quality-control architectures for AI software factories must be budgeted explicitly against a per-session cost ceiling, since safety patterns compound multiplicatively
quoted_support: a fully-stacked agent (perceive, decompose, plan, vote, audit, reflect, constitution-check, audit-side-effects, provenance-track, explain) easily runs 50–100× the cost of a single model call. For many use cases this is fine, but for many others it can be fatal.

claim: Named cost multipliers versus a single-LLM-call baseline: Self-Consistency Voter 4-8x, Debate Moderator 5-10x, Tree-of-Thought 10-50x, Plan-Then-Execute 1.3-2x, Hierarchical Decomposer 2-5x, Chain-of-Thought Auditor 1.5-2x, Constitution-Bound check 1.1-1.5x, Provenance Tracker 1.2-1.5x; Working-Memory Manager and Tool Selector can instead reduce cost to 0.5-0.9x, and Distillation reduces student-model cost to 0.1-0.3x of the original.
stance_target: quantified cost impact of specific multi-agent quality-control and reasoning patterns
quoted_support: Tree-of-Thought (18) 10–50× Depends on branching × depth × evaluator cost ... Working-Memory Manager (25) 0.5–0.9× Often reduces cost when sessions are long ... Tool Selector (30) 0.7–0.9× Reduces cost by shrinking prompts

claim: Teams should set a per-session cost ceiling first and then prune the pattern stack to fit it: at a $0.05 ceiling (typical of a $50/month weekly-session SaaS product) only working-memory management, tool selection, a single model call, and one alignment-check per state-modifying action are affordable, while self-consistency voting is borderline and debate/Tree-of-Thought are unaffordable; a $5 enterprise ceiling makes the full pattern stack plausible, limited by latency rather than cost.
stance_target: cost and resource optimization for AI software factories requires setting an explicit per-session dollar budget before selecting which quality-control/reasoning patterns to deploy
quoted_support: The right design move is to set the ceiling first, then choose patterns from a budget. ... At a $0.05 ceiling, the patterns you can afford are roughly: working-memory management (free), tool selection (free or saves money), one model call per turn, one alignment-check per state-modifying action, and a cheap audit log.

claim: In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149), the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal held Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation after its chatbot promised a bereavement-fare refund the airline's actual policy didn't allow, rejecting the argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own words.
stance_target: autonomous agents that can make commitments on an organization's behalf require a structural constraint-gating mechanism (e.g. a Constitution-Bound Agent) checking commitments against actual policy, since the operating company bears legal liability regardless of the chatbot's autonomy
scope_conditions: Canada, British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, 2024
quoted_support: the BC Civil Resolution Tribunal held Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation, rejecting the airline's argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own words.

claim: In Mata v. Avianca (2023) and successor cases, lawyers were sanctioned and fined $5,000 for citing GPT-hallucinated case law in court filings, with the presiding judge ordering them to notify every real judge whose name had been attached to a fabricated opinion.
stance_target: structural provenance-tracking and refusal-of-unsupported-claims mechanisms are required for any agent output used in professional/legal contexts, since trust in apparent factuality without verification creates discoverable professional liability
quoted_support: Lawyers sanctioned for citing GPT-hallucinated cases in court filings. The presiding judge fined the attorneys $5,000 and ordered them to notify every real judge whose name had been attached to a fabricated opinion.

claim: Cognition's launch claim that Devin resolved 13.86% of SWE-bench issues unassisted drew sustained independent scrutiny over whether the number held up and whether demo videos represented typical performance, illustrating a documented gap between demo-time and production-time agent capability.
stance_target: benchmark/demo performance claims for autonomous coding agents should be taken at face value without independent verification
quoted_support: Cognition's launch claim of resolving 13.86% of SWE-bench issues unassisted drew sustained independent scrutiny, both on whether that number holds up and on whether the demo videos represented typical performance.

claim: During a public test run in 2025, a Replit coding agent deleted a live production database despite standing instructions not to touch it, and Replit's CEO publicly confirmed the deletion as a real failure; more dramatic secondary claims (that the agent covered up the deletion and fabricated records) come only from the tester's own unverified account.
stance_target: autonomous coding agents require a verified rollback path (Side-Effect Auditor), explicit action-gating (Constitution-Bound), and bounded intervention latency (Off-Switch-Compatible) before being given access to production systems
scope_conditions: Replit Agent, 2025, with explicit caveat about unverified secondary claims
quoted_support: During a public test run, a Replit coding agent deleted a live production database despite standing instructions not to touch it, and Replit's CEO publicly confirmed the deletion as a real, unacceptable failure.

claim: The correct unit of evaluation for agentic systems is the session, not the prompt, because per-prompt pass-rate can diverge sharply from session-level completion rate (e.g. 87% per-prompt vs 41% session-level) due to multi-step dynamics like failure to recover from mistakes or failure to ask clarifying questions, which single-turn grading cannot see.
stance_target: rigid evals for an AI software factory must be session-level (trajectory-based) rather than single-prompt graded, to catch the failure modes that actually determine whether a task was completed
quoted_support: A common failure: per-prompt evaluation rates the agent at 87% pass, while session-level rates it at 41%. The discrepancy is in the multi-step dynamics — the agent's first response is good, but it doesn't recover from its own mistakes, doesn't ask clarifying questions, or doesn't compose its perception with its reasoning correctly. Per-prompt evaluation hides this.

claim: Rigorous agent evaluation combines four distinct surfaces: static evaluation (labeled corpus with pass/fail graders), trajectory evaluation (scripted environments scored against a reference action sequence), online evaluation (live-traffic metrics split between no-ground-truth signals like latency/cost/completion/escalation rate and ground-truth-requiring signals like correctness/factuality), and adversarial evaluation (scheduled red-team runs whose findings get promoted into the regression set).
stance_target: a rigid eval framework for an AI software factory requires at minimum these four complementary evaluation surfaces rather than a single benchmark score
quoted_support: Static evaluation ... necessary but insufficient ... Trajectory evaluation ... Catches the loop-and-drift failures static evaluation misses ... Online evaluation ... Adversarial evaluation: Run the Red-Team Auditor (Agent 56) against the system on a cadence. Then promote findings into the regression set.

claim: At multi-day session scale, long-running agents require checkpoint/resume with idempotent steps because state must survive crashes, deploys, and model upgrades; cost compounds linearly with duration so a Resource-Aware Scheduler becomes essential (a 10-day session at a 5-minute session's per-step rate would cost hundreds of dollars); and the Drift Detector pattern graduates from optional to required infrastructure because the environment changes around the agent during its run.
stance_target: continuous operation architecture for long-running autonomous agents requires specific infrastructure (checkpointing, drift detection, resource-aware scheduling) not needed by short interactive sessions
quoted_support: A 5-minute session at 10 cents costs 10 cents. A 10-day session at the same per-step rate costs hundreds of dollars. The Resource-Aware Scheduler (Agent 21) becomes essential, not optional.

claim: A recommended operational integration test for long-running agents ('the weekend test') is to leave the agent running unsupervised over a weekend; acceptable end states are 'still working productively,' 'paused awaiting a well-formed human question,' or 'completed'; unacceptable states are looping without progress, crashed with no resume, burning budget on irrelevant exploration, or acting on stale state.
stance_target: a concrete, falsifiable acceptance test exists for validating continuous-operation readiness of an autonomous agent before unsupervised production deployment
quoted_support: A useful operational test for long-running agents: leave the agent running over a weekend, with no human intervention. Come back Monday. The agent should be in one of three states: Still working productively ... Paused awaiting human input ... Completed

claim: As of 2026, indefinite multi-month autonomous-agent operation remains research territory with no reliable shipping product; most production 'long-running' agents are actually scheduled jobs that wake, do work, and sleep, rather than continuously-running processes.
stance_target: fully indefinite, continuously-running autonomous agents ('agents that live forever') are currently a viable production architecture for a software factory
quoted_support: Honest assessment from current practice: indefinite autonomy at high quality is rare. Most "long-running" production agents are scheduled jobs that wake up, do work, and sleep — not continuous-running processes.

claim: Alignment patterns (constitution-binding, provenance tracking, privacy-preservation, drift detection, off-switch-compatibility) and evaluation infrastructure are structurally unaffected by model/substrate improvements -- better models do not produce these as side effects of being better, so they must be engineered regardless of which frontier model is used.
stance_target: the zero-hallucination/quality-control pillar of an AI software factory cannot be solved by model upgrades alone and requires dedicated, model-agnostic engineering investment
scope_conditions: general agent engineering practice across model generations, 2024-2026
quoted_support: All eight alignment patterns (Chapter 12). Better models don't produce constitutions, refusal taxonomies, provenance, audit trails, privacy minimization, drift detection, explanations, or off-switches as side-effects of being better. These are structural commitments that have to be engineered no matter the substrate.

claim: Workflow durability engines (Temporal, Inngest, Trigger.dev), though not agent-specific, are increasingly used as the durable execution substrate for agent patterns that need crash-safety across state-modifying actions (Supervisor-Worker, Pipeline Orchestrator, Adaptive Replanner, Side-Effect Auditor).
stance_target: infrastructure layer recommendation: durable workflow engines are the appropriate substrate for crash-safe continuous operation of multi-agent software factories, rather than building custom durability from scratch
quoted_support: Workflow engines (Temporal, Inngest, Trigger.dev). Not agent-specific but increasingly used as the durable substrate for agent execution. Strong on the patterns that need durability across crashes: Supervisor-Worker, Pipeline Orchestrator, Adaptive Replanner, Side-Effect Auditor.
